Modern.brandNameRationale: Acuity is a real Latin-rooted word meaning sharpness of thought, vision, or hearing. It signals precision and clarity without being literal about education. Modern.manifesto: Most online learning platforms confuse breadth with depth. Ten thousand courses, infinite trees of topics, a recommendation engine that nobody asked for. Minimal.brandNameRationale: Folio is a real word meaning a sheet of paper folded once, and historically a book of large format. In a learning context, it suggests both the page (the lesson) and the binding (the curriculum). One uncommon Latin-rooted word, like Notion or Linear. Reads as quiet, considered, slightly archaic.
Minimal.manifesto: Online learning platforms have grown into video-heavy, gamified, notification-driven products. We made Folio because the actual material of learning is still the page — a sheet you can read, mark up, return to. Each lesson is a folio. The product is the folio reader. No video, no quizzes, no streaks.
Minimal.industrySummary: Self-paced learning has become video-first and gamified. There is real space for a minimal platform that returns to the page as the unit — closer to a digital textbook than a video course.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Brilliant (brilliant.org) plays in the modern self-paced slot. Maven (maven.com) holds the live-cohort middle. Sub-stack-style writers (Lenny's Newsletter and similar) play in the single-author space. We sit further out — fewer features, the page is the product.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Folio is a self-paced learning platform where each lesson is a single readable sheet — no video, no quizzes, no gamification.
Minimal.positioningRationale: We strip the learning surface to text and annotation. The reader marks up the folio. The folio stays in the library.

Corporate.industrySummary: Enterprise education infrastructure (LMS, SIS, student lifecycle systems) is dominated by a small number of incumbents (Blackboard, Canvas, PowerSchool). The opening is for a serious mid-tier vendor with implementation depth, contract flexibility, and the procurement-friendly posture institutional buyers demand.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: PowerSchool (powerschool.com) is the K-12 incumbent. Instructure (instructure.com) holds the higher-ed reference. Blackboard (blackboard.com) is the legacy peer. We belong in the regional mid-tier institutional vendor category.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Lectern Education Group provides LMS, SIS, and learner analytics platforms to K-12 districts, higher-ed institutions, and adult-learning providers.

Corporate.mission: To provide a serious operating platform for mid-tier education brands that want to keep their identity and outsource the operations.

coreValues: Senior — partners deal with partners.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Westlake is a real American place-name with a heritage trade register. Education Holdings follows the multi-brand operator naming convention used in education. The pair reads as an institutional operator with multi-brand portfolio scale.
Corporate.manifesto: Westlake Education Holdings owns and operates a portfolio of education brands. Corporate.industrySummary: Education has consolidated under a small number of multi-brand operators. The opening underneath is for a regional mid-tier multi-brand operator with deep operations.

Corporate.positioningStatement: Westlake Education Holdings is a regional multi-brand education operator running shared sourcing, operations, and distribution across a portfolio of brands.

Creative.tagline: Courses for people who want to learn something old.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Curriculum is the foundational academic term for a course of study. The definite article + Co suffix follows the considered-creative trade-name school.
Creative.manifesto: Most edtech brands sell certificates, transformations, and career changes. We made Night School because some people want to learn things for the same reason they read books: because it's interesting. The brand is for evening classes, weekend workshops, and the kind of learning that doesn't appear on a LinkedIn profile.
Creative.industrySummary: Edtech branding has been polished, credential-led, and slightly anxious. There's room for a brand that's warm, playful, sticker-friendly, and serious about the older tradition of learning-for-its-own-sake.
Creative.competitorLandscape: School of Life (theschooloflife.com) holds the closest cultural-learning peer. MasterClass (masterclass.com) does the celebrity-led version. The Strand's classes do the bookstore-adjacent middle. We sit warmer and louder than any of them.
Creative.positioningStatement: Learning for adults who want it for the love of it.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 50. Successful in their day job. Already reads two books a month. Wants to take a class for fun. Doesn't need a certificate. Tells friends about the class at dinner.

dos: Make jokes about credentialism
Quote real student stories
Talk to the adult who's already curious

Creative.tagline: A small school for unusual subjects.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Owl is the academic-tradition symbol of wisdom; inkwell is the tradition's writing object. Pairing them with an ampersand creates a name that reads as a small academy or independent school, slightly literary, slightly old-fashioned. The pairing borrows from the bookshop-and-academy naming tradition (Hatchard & Co, Lutyens & Rubinstein) without imitating any of them.
Creative.manifesto: Most online education sells employable skills. We started Owl & Inkwell because the actual best learning is often unemployable — Latin etymology, medieval astronomy, the history of paper, the lost art of letter-writing. We run small live courses on subjects that will not improve your career and may improve your life. The school exists because the subject does.
Creative.industrySummary: Online education has consolidated around career-utility courses. There is real space for an unapologetically non-utility platform — courses in the humanities, classics, history, and craft, taught by enthusiasts to small live cohorts.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Hardcore History (dancarlin.com) plays in the long-form humanities space. London Writers Salon (londonwriterssalon.com) holds the small-academy peer slot. Catapult (catapult.co) sits in the writing-school middle. We sit alongside Catapult with a broader humanities footprint and a clearer literary register.
Creative.positioningStatement: Owl & Inkwell is a small live-course school offering courses in the humanities, classics, history, and craft — taught for love, not for career.
Creative.positioningRationale: The brand stakes a position against career-utility learning. Course descriptions argue for the subject on its own terms. The audience is self-selecting.

targetAudience.primary: Adults 30–65 who read for pleasure and learn for love.
behaviors: Read history, poetry, and essays for fun.
Sign up for one-off lectures and reading groups.
motivations: Want to learn a subject for its own sake.
Want a small live class with real conversation.
Want a teacher who loves the subject.

dos: Write course descriptions like a friend recommending a book.
Reference the teacher's pet enthusiasms.
Print the schedule on a card.
Sign emails by the teacher who designed the course.

messagingPillars.name: Subjects worth learning
messagingPillars.description: Each course is a six to ten week live cohort on a subject the teacher loves — Roman roads, the history of bookbinding, Anglo-Saxon poetry, beekeeping.

messagingPillars.name: The reading list
messagingPillars.description: Every course comes with a printed reading list mailed to students. The list is the course; the live sessions are the conversation.

messagingPillars.name: Small live cohorts
messagingPillars.description: Cohorts cap at thirty. The teacher knows every student's name by the second session.

Creative.tagline: A learning platform where the course materials are open.
Creative.brandDescription: The Open Course Co is a creative-led learning platform that publishes all course materials openly under permissive licenses, with revenue from live cohort participation rather than from the materials.
Creative.scope:
The Open Course Co works across:
• Course materials published openly under permissive licenses
• Revenue from live cohort participation and instructor-led discussion
• Quarterly published essays on open education
• Open-source course-platform tooling
• Annual community gathering
Creative.mission: To treat course materials as a public good and live instruction as the work.
Creative.vision: A platform whose course materials become standard references for serious learning.
coreValues: Warm — open materials are a public good.
Specific — every material is licensed openly.
Considered — paid instruction is the revenue.
Literary — the writing about open education is part of the platform.
Creative.brandNameRationale: The Open Course is the universal phrase for openly-licensed educational material. Naming the platform after the principle stakes a clear creative position. The definite article + Co suffix follows the considered-creative trade-name school.
Creative.manifesto: Most learning platforms protect their course materials and sell access. We started The Open Course Co because the actual most useful learning model is open materials and paid live instruction.
Creative.industrySummary: Online learning treats course materials as proprietary. There is real space for a creative-led platform that publishes openly and charges for live instruction.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Khan Academy (khanacademy.org) plays the open-content peer at scale. MIT OpenCourseWare (ocw.mit.edu) holds the open-academic peer slot. Free Code Camp (freecodecamp.org) sits in the open-tech peer position. We sit alongside Khan Academy with paid live cohorts.
Creative.positioningStatement: The Open Course Co is a learning platform with openly-licensed course materials and revenue from live cohort participation.
Creative.positioningRationale: The brand competes on the open premise. Every course, every essay, every cohort is built around open materials and paid live discussion.
